passage.title: The Hidden Cost of Free Public Transport

paragraphs.text: For more than forty years, riders in Halbrook, a fictional city of about four hundred thousand people, paid for every bus and tram journey, first with coins and later with plastic cards. Then the city council voted to abolish fares across the whole network. Ticket machines were removed from vehicles, and the turnstiles at the main tram stations were left permanently open. The council gave two reasons for the change: it would help residents on low incomes reach work and services, and it would persuade drivers to leave their cars at home.

The first months seemed to confirm both hopes. Automatic counters on the vehicles recorded far more boardings than in the same months of the previous year, and local newspapers printed photographs of full trams. Officials explained the increase in the simplest way available. People who had once driven were now riding, they said, and people who had once stayed home because of the cost were finally traveling. Few questioned this account, since rising ridership was exactly what the policy had been designed to produce.

Doubts arrived from several directions at once. Traffic counts on the main roads into the city center had barely changed, which was difficult to reconcile with a large shift away from cars. Complaints about overcrowding rose, and some long-time riders reported that buses passed them at peak hours because there was no room. A short survey at tram stops added a further puzzle: many of the new trips were journeys of only a few stops, which riders said they had previously made on foot or by bicycle.

To find out what was happening, a team at the transit agency combined three kinds of records. Sensor counts showed where and when people boarded. Travel diaries kept for a week by a sample of households showed how trips had changed and why. Service records showed how many vehicles had actually run on each route. Putting these sources side by side revealed a clear geographical pattern. Growth was concentrated on the frequent central routes, while ridership on the routes serving outer districts had changed very little.

The records also explained the crowding. Fares had once covered part of the cost of running the system, and the city replaced only some of that lost revenue from its general budget. With no additional money, the agency added no vehicles, so the extra riders were squeezed into roughly the same number of buses and trams. On the outer routes, buses still came only every thirty or forty minutes. A free journey on a bus that arrives too late for a morning shift offers little to someone who must be at work on time.

The decisive turn came when the team examined who paid for the policy and who benefited. Because the replacement funding came from general taxes, every household contributed. The largest savings, however, went to residents of central districts who already rode often, a group that included many people with moderate or high incomes. Low-income residents of the outer districts gained less than expected. Many had previously qualified for discounted passes, so their savings were small, and the infrequent service meant that free fares rarely changed whether a trip was possible.

Some questions remained open. Driving habits can take years to change, and a later study might find that car use eventually fell. The team therefore proposed measuring the policy by more than boardings: the time people waited, how often vehicles were too full to board, and how many jobs residents could reach within forty-five minutes. They also suggested comparing the actual policy with an alternative that would have spent the same money on more frequent service, so that the value of free fares could be judged against a realistic choice.

Looking back, the sequence of discoveries separates what was seen from what it was taken to mean. The observations were more boardings, crowded central routes, little change on outer routes, and savings that flowed mostly to frequent riders. The interpretation the team drew was that the policy lowered the price of travel without making travel more available. That conclusion concerns Halbrook under its particular funding decisions; it does not show that free transport fails everywhere. It does show that a free trip is of little use when it cannot be taken at the time it is needed.

passage.title: Why Sleep Does Not Simply Store Memories

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, sleep was often treated in memory research as a kind of protective pause. Early observations suggested that people who slept after learning tended to forget less than those who stayed awake, and a common interpretation was that sleep simply shielded fresh memories from the interference of new experiences. Over the following decades, that picture changed. Sleep came to be understood not as an empty interval but as a period of organized brain activity, and researchers from several fields began to ask what that activity actually does to memories.

From the viewpoint of researchers who study memory consolidation, sleep actively strengthens and reorganizes what was learned during the day. Recordings in animals have shown that patterns of brain activity seen during learning can reappear during later sleep, a phenomenon often described as replay. On this view, replay helps integrate recent experiences into longer-lasting networks. Experiments in which people perform better on certain tasks after a night of sleep than after an equal period awake are commonly interpreted as support for this active role.

A second group of researchers approaches the question at the level of connections between neurons. Their concern is that waking experience tends to strengthen many connections, and such strengthening cannot continue indefinitely without costs in energy and capacity. One influential proposal, known as the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, suggests that sleep broadly weakens connections, restoring the brain's ability to learn the next day. This perspective faces a practical constraint: connection strength is difficult to measure directly in humans, so much of its evidence comes from animal studies.

Despite their different starting points, the two perspectives agree on several observations. For many kinds of material, sleep after learning is associated with better retention than an equivalent period of wakefulness. Brain activity during sleep is organized rather than random, and it is linked in some way to what happened during the preceding day. Both groups also accept that sleep does more than reduce interference, which means that the older idea of a protective pause cannot account for the findings on its own.

The perspectives divide, however, over a further finding: not all memories benefit equally from sleep. If sleep mainly strengthens memories, uneven benefits require an additional explanation, such as some memories being replayed more often than others. If sleep mainly weakens connections overall, uneven benefits could arise because weaker traces fall below a threshold and fade, while stronger ones survive in relative terms. The same observation can thus be described as selective strengthening or as selective loss, and the two descriptions point to different mechanisms.

A third perspective, from researchers interested in how memory serves future behavior, reframes the issue. Studies have reported that the benefit of sleep can be greater for information people expect to need later, or for items they were told to remember rather than forget. From this viewpoint, sleep may act less like a storage device than like a filter that favors what is likely to be useful. This framing does not decide between strengthening and weakening; instead, it asks what determines which memories are favored in the first place.

Each perspective therefore reads forgetting differently. For consolidation researchers, forgetting is largely a side effect of what is not replayed. For synaptic researchers, some forgetting is part of sleep's function, since weakening is how capacity is restored. For those focused on future relevance, forgetting is the other half of selection. The views are compatible in treating sleep as active and selective, and some researchers propose that broad weakening and targeted strengthening could both occur during sleep. They remain in tension, however, over which process does most of the work.

What can be stated with some confidence is narrower than the popular image of sleep filing away the day's memories. Sleep appears to change memories rather than merely preserve them, and the changes are uneven, with some information favored and some allowed to fade. How that unevenness arises, and whether forgetting is better seen as a purpose or as a by-product, remain open questions. The role of sleep is better described as reshaping memory than as storing it, although the details of that reshaping are still being worked out.

passage.title: The Unexpected Effects of Public Rankings

paragraphs.text: The office described here is invented, but the question it raises can be examined with evidence. Imagine a city service office that begins posting a monthly ranking of its departments on a hallway screen, scoring each one on the share of its cases closed within a target time. Within three months, almost every department's score has improved. Over the same period, however, residents whose requests involve more than one department begin complaining that they are passed from desk to desk. Why would a measure that seems to make each department faster leave the office as a whole less cooperative?

One explanation focuses on incentives. The ranking counts only what each department finishes on its own, so a shared case that requires waiting for another team becomes a liability. Staff who want a good score may reasonably set such cases aside or hand them on quickly. On this account, no one has become less willing to help; people are responding sensibly to what is counted. The hypothesis makes a clear prediction: cooperation should fall mainly on tasks that affect the score, and it should return soon after the score is changed.

A second explanation focuses on relationships. Publishing the scores where everyone can see them turns colleagues into competitors; a department near the bottom may feel embarrassed, while one near the top may feel watched. Rivalry of this kind can reduce goodwill in general, not only on scored tasks. If this account is right, staff should also become less likely to share information informally or answer quick questions, although neither appears in the ranking. Recovery should also be slower, because trust is not restored by a change of formula.

The hypotheses thus diverge at three points. The first concerns help that the ranking does not record: incentives alone give staff little reason to stop answering a colleague's phone call, while rivalry gives them some. The second concerns timing, since incentive effects should follow changes in the rules closely, whereas effects on relationships may linger. The third concerns position in the list. If embarrassment and pride matter, departments at the top and bottom might behave differently even under identical rules, a difference the incentive account would not particularly expect.

Interpreting the case is harder than these predictions suggest, because the improvement in scores is itself ambiguous. Some may reflect genuine effort, such as clearing backlogs. Some may reflect changes in recording, for example closing a request and opening a new one whenever it has to move elsewhere. Both hypotheses can accommodate either possibility. Faster scores combined with slower shared cases are exactly what the incentive account predicts, but rivalry that made departments reluctant to depend on one another would produce the same pattern.

Suppose the office then adds a joint indicator: shared cases are scored by how quickly they are completed overall, and every department involved receives the same result. In this imagined account, shared cases speed up within a few weeks. A staff survey, however, shows that informal requests for help remain below their earlier level for several months. The incentive account explains the first finding easily, since the new score rewards finishing shared cases. The relationship account explains the second, since a shared number does not by itself undo the habits of rivalry the ranking encouraged.

Neither result settles the matter. The quick change in shared cases might partly reflect a warmer atmosphere, and the slow recovery of informal help might reflect busy schedules rather than lingering mistrust. More decisive evidence would come from a change that separates the two mechanisms. If the office stopped displaying the ranking but kept reporting each department's scores privately to its own manager, the incentives would stay roughly the same while the public comparison disappeared. A return of informal help under those conditions would strengthen the relationship account; no change would favor the incentive account.

What the case supports, then, is limited. Staff behavior shifted after the ranking appeared, both on shared cases and, according to the survey, in informal help, so it is reasonable to say that the act of measuring changed what people did. Which mechanism did most of the work cannot be determined from the observations described, and both may have contributed. Nor can an invented office show how rankings will affect other organizations. For this office, at least, the scores alone would have given a misleading picture of what the ranking achieved.

passage.title: Why Giant Animals Disappeared Differently

paragraphs.text: If one cause had removed the largest land animals of the late Ice Age, a simple test would follow: the losses should line up with that cause wherever it appeared. Between roughly fifty thousand and ten thousand years ago, many species of mammoths, giant ground sloths, and other large animals disappeared, while most smaller animals survived. Scientists have long debated whether hunting by people or changes in climate were responsible. Framing the question as a choice between the two, however, assumes that the extinctions were a single event requiring a single explanation.

The first component is the arrival of modern humans. Large animals are especially vulnerable to added hunting because they typically reproduce slowly; a species that raises one young every few years cannot quickly replace adults that are killed. Even modest hunting, sustained over centuries, could push such a population into decline without any dramatic slaughter. This mechanism predicts that extinctions should follow human arrival in each region, and that the largest, slowest-breeding species should be lost most often.

The second component is climate. As the last glacial period ended, temperatures and rainfall shifted, sometimes abruptly, and grasslands, forests, and wetlands moved or shrank. Animals that depended on particular vegetation could find their ranges broken into smaller, more isolated pieces. A population confined to a few scattered patches is easier to find and less able to recover from losses than one spread across a continuous landscape. Each pressure, in other words, can increase the damage done by the other.

A third component determines how strongly the first two act: the history of each place. In Africa, where large animals had lived alongside human ancestors for an extremely long time, comparatively many survived. Islands present the opposite boundary case. Animals there often evolved without large predators, and on islands that people reached only recently, such as New Zealand, large birds disappeared within a few centuries of human arrival, long after the Ice Age had ended. Such cases set limits on any explanation that ties the losses to a single period of climate change.

Because these components varied from region to region, similar losses could arise from different combinations. In Australia, many large animals disappeared after people arrived tens of thousands of years ago, at a time for which many researchers find no climate shift as sharp as the one near the end of the Ice Age. In North America, by contrast, human arrival and rapid climate change came close together, so the two pressures overlapped. In northern Eurasia, where people had been present much longer, some large animals persisted until warming reduced their habitats and only then declined.

Comparing the timing of these events turns the regional differences into evidence. Researchers use dated bones to estimate when species were last present and compare those dates with evidence of human arrival and climate change. If losses repeatedly cluster after human arrival regardless of climate, hunting gains support; if they cluster at climate shifts regardless of people, climate does. The emerging pattern fits neither expectation completely. Timing cannot prove a cause, since two events can coincide by chance, and the youngest bone found rarely belongs to the last animal that lived. It can, however, rule out explanations that predict the wrong order of events.

Asking what happens when only one factor changes clarifies the mechanism. Where people arrived without major climate change, as on many islands, extinctions still occurred, suggesting that hunting alone could be enough for vulnerable species. Where climate changed sharply without people, as during earlier warm periods of the Ice Age, many large animals appear to have survived. Climate alone, then, was seldom decisive, while its effects became more dangerous once hunting was added. A small population of mammoths on a remote Arctic island, which lasted thousands of years after the mainland herds vanished, is often read the same way: distance from people mattered.

Did a single cause, then, remove the giant animals? The comparison of regions and dates suggests that it did not, at least not in the same way everywhere. Human hunting appears to have been the most consistent element, yet its effects depended on climate, on the size and breeding rate of each species, and on how long animals had lived alongside people. The extinctions are better understood as regional outcomes produced by shared components combined in different proportions. What the evidence supports is not a single culprit but a pattern of interaction.

passage.title: A Village That Shared Water but Not Risk

paragraphs.text: Is a rule that gives every farmer the same amount of water a fair rule? The question can be tested against a case, and the case examined here is imaginary: an irrigation association in a hill village we will call Tessaro, whose members all draw water from a single canal. The claim worth examining is the one the association itself repeated for decades: that because each household received an identical share, no household could reasonably complain of being treated unfairly.

The rule was simple. Every member received the canal's full flow for the same number of hours each week, regardless of the size or location of their fields. Turns rotated, so no family was permanently first or last. The arrangement grew out of earlier disputes in which larger landholders had taken more than their share, and older members remembered its adoption as a victory. Equal hours were also easy to check: anyone could stand by the sluice gate and see whose turn it was.

The arguments for the rule are stronger than they might first appear. Equal shares need no expert to calculate them, so they resist manipulation by whoever controls the measurements. They treat members as equals within the association, which matters in a village where status once decided access. They are also predictable: a farmer can plan planting around a known schedule. A more complicated formula might be fairer in theory, yet in practice it could invite exactly the suspicion that the equal rule was designed to remove.

The strongest objection concerns what equal water does on unequal land. Fields near the upper end of the canal have deep soil that holds moisture; fields at the lower end are sandy and drain quickly. In a dry year, the same number of hours keeps an upper field alive but leaves a lower field parched. The rule distributes water equally, yet it distributes the damage of drought very unequally. On this view, the association treated the input as the thing to be shared while ignoring the outcomes that families actually lived with.

This objection, however, holds only under certain conditions. In wet years, when every field receives enough water, differences in soil hardly matter, and the equal rule produces roughly similar harvests. The objection also assumes that lower-field families did not choose their land knowing its risks. Where fields were inherited rather than bought at a discount, that assumption seems reasonable. The objection is therefore strongest in drought, and among families who had no realistic way to avoid poor soil.

Some members proposed a compensation scheme: in years of severe drought, upper-field households would contribute part of their harvest to a fund for lower-field households. Supporters saw it as correcting outcomes without abandoning equal water. Critics noted that it reintroduced the problem the old rule had solved, since someone must decide what counts as severe drought and how losses are measured. The proposal does not settle the dispute in favor of either side. What it shows is that correcting unequal outcomes requires judgments the simple rule avoided.

Both sides also overlook certain cases. A lower-field family that switched to drought-tolerant crops might suffer less than an upper-field family that planted thirsty ones; compensation based on location alone would then help the wrong household. Conversely, an upper field could be damaged by flooding in an unusually wet year, a risk that the debate about drought ignores entirely. Risk depends on both land and choices, and neither equal hours nor location-based compensation tracks that combination perfectly.

What the Tessaro case establishes is a distinction rather than a verdict. Equal treatment in allocating a resource is not the same as fairness in the burdens people bear as a result. That much seems secure: identical shares can produce very unequal harms when conditions differ. What remains uncertain is how far an association should go in correcting those harms, given that every correction depends on measurements that can be disputed. The answer to the opening question is therefore conditional: an equal rule can be fair as a procedure while being unfair in its effects.

passage.title: How Charts Can Hide a Trend

paragraphs.text: Two charts lie side by side, and every number in them is the same. Both show the monthly average wait at the public clinics of Larkford, a city invented for this example, over three years, during which the average rose from 21 to 25 minutes. On the first chart the vertical axis runs from 0 to 60 minutes, and the line looks almost flat. On the second the axis runs from 20 to 26, and the same line climbs steeply. Neither chart contains a false figure, yet readers describe them in opposite ways.

For years, Larkford's communications office printed the first version in its quarterly newsletter. The 0-to-60 axis was simply the default setting of its software; nobody had selected it in order to reassure residents. The situation changed when a council member, preparing for a budget debate, posted the second version online under the caption that waits were soaring. Many residents who remembered the flat line felt misled, and their anger was directed less at the council member than at the office that had shown them the calm picture.

The office's first response was to defend its chart. The numbers were identical, staff pointed out, and starting an axis at zero is a widely taught rule. That rule, however, applies chiefly to bar charts, where the length of each bar must be proportional to the value it represents; a line chart conveys change through its slope, and a zero baseline is not required. The defence persuaded few people. Complaints increased, because insisting that the figures were correct did nothing to address the impression that residents had formed.

The turning point came when staff stopped asking which chart was honest and asked instead what size of change mattered. A rise of four minutes is roughly one-fifth of the starting value. The zero-based chart made that change nearly invisible, while the narrow axis made it resemble an emergency. Each chart had quietly answered a question that readers had not been asked: how large must a change be before it counts as important? The reversal of impressions came from that hidden judgment, built into the choice of axis but never stated.

The office then tried a series of changes. First, each chart was accompanied by a plain sentence: the average wait rose from 21 to 25 minutes, or about one-fifth, over three years. Next, the axis range was tied to a stated reference, the clinics' own target of 30 minutes, which appeared as a horizontal line on a scale from 0 to 40. Finally, a small panel of residents was asked to describe draft charts before publication, and any chart was revised when the panel's descriptions differed from the accompanying sentence.

For a while the changes seemed to work. Panel descriptions converged, and complaints declined. Then an unexpected problem appeared. With the target line in view, readers judged the trend by its distance from 30 minutes, and an average still below the target looked reassuring. Meanwhile, the share of patients waiting more than an hour had doubled from a small base, a change the average concealed. The fix for one framing problem had moved attention to the target, and that choice, too, determined what readers noticed.

Comparing the stages makes the shift in understanding clearer. At first, the misleading element was a default that nobody had examined. During the dispute, attention narrowed to the range of the axis. Later, the office recognized that its choices extended further: to which measure was shown, which reference line was drawn, and which words accompanied the picture. Its current newsletter presents two charts, one for the average wait and one for long waits, each with a short explanation of why its scale was chosen.

What happened in Larkford can be stated as observation: identical and correct numbers produced opposite impressions depending on the axis, and a later reference line changed which trend readers noticed. The interpretation is broader. Accurate figures are necessary for an honest chart, but they are not sufficient, because the frame of a chart makes its own claims about which changes deserve attention. Whether a given frame misleads depends on the question a reader brings to it, and a chart that leaves that question unstated leaves the answer to the design.

passage.title: When Flood Walls Move the Water Elsewhere

paragraphs.text: In the spring of an unusually wet year, the town of Fennick, a fictional settlement on the upper reaches of the equally fictional Calder River, stayed dry for the first time in a generation. Thirty kilometers downstream, the village of Ashby flooded twice within a month, although the rain that fell there was no heavier than in earlier wet years. Residents of Ashby could point to the high-water marks painted on their church wall: the new ones stood above the old. One community had been spared, while another, receiving similar rainfall, had suffered more than before.

The result needs to be stated with care. It does not show that Fennick's good fortune directly caused every flood in Ashby, nor that Ashby would otherwise have stayed dry. The village had flooded before. What changed was how often its floods occurred and how high they rose in years whose rainfall resembled earlier ones. A common misunderstanding is to treat such a pattern as bad luck, since rainfall varies. But if the rain was similar and the floods were worse, something about the river had changed between the two places.

The most direct clue came from the regional water authority's records. Gauges along the river showed that peak flows at Ashby were now arriving sooner and reaching higher levels than they had during comparable storms in the past. Partly in response, planners had begun to consider a basin-wide system of retention areas, low fields that could be allowed to flood temporarily and hold water back. Their interest pointed in the same direction as the gauges: the water reaching Ashby was no longer being held anywhere along its path.

Going one step further back, the question becomes where that water used to go. In earlier decades, the land along the river between Fennick and Ashby included broad meadows that flooded during heavy rain. These meadows did not prevent floods so much as slow them, spreading the water out so that it drained downstream over days rather than hours. A river with room to spread delivers a lower, later peak than one confined to a narrow channel, even when the total volume of water is the same.

The background condition, then, was the gradual loss of that room. Over several decades, many meadows upstream of Ashby were drained for housing and farming, and much of the remaining land was protected by embankments. Each step made sense to the landowners concerned, and none of them on its own seemed significant. Together, however, they changed how the river behaved. Water that had once paused across the floodplain was now carried through a confined channel, and the downstream village received it faster and in greater concentration.

Tracing the chain back to its beginning leads to Fennick's flood walls. After a damaging flood years earlier, the town raised its embankments along the riverbank, sealing off the last meadows within its boundaries. The walls worked exactly as intended: they kept water out of Fennick's streets. But the water they excluded did not disappear. It continued downstream, joined by extra flow from other stretches that had also lost their floodplain, and arrived at Ashby, which had no comparable defenses of its own.

Could the same result have come about another way? Possibly. Changes in farming upstream, such as soil that absorbs less rain, could also increase runoff, and new roads and roofs in Ashby itself could worsen local flooding. These alternatives cannot be ruled out entirely. They would not easily explain, however, why the higher peaks arrived earlier at Ashby during the very storms that left Fennick dry, a timing pattern that fits the loss of upstream storage more closely.

Reconstructed in order, the sequence runs from a reasonable local decision to a regional cost. Fennick optimized protection for its own streets and, by its own measure, succeeded. The basin as a whole, however, lost storage that had once served every community along the river. What can be observed directly is the dry town, the flooded village, and the changed gauge readings. That the walls formed a major link in the chain is an interpretation, though one supported by several kinds of evidence; how much each factor contributed would require further study.

passage.title: The Difference Between Equality and Fairness

paragraphs.text: At a table of four colleagues, a large pizza was cut into eight equal slices, and each person took two. Nobody objected. A week later the same colleagues ordered the same pizza, cut it the same way, and the evening ended in a quiet argument. The pizza had not changed, and neither had the method of dividing it. What had changed was the situation of the people around the table. The contrast between the two evenings is small, but it raises a question that reaches well beyond shared meals: what, exactly, had made the first division feel fair?

On the first evening, equal shares seemed fair almost automatically. Everyone had paid the same amount, everyone was about equally hungry, and no one had a stronger claim than anyone else. Under those conditions, treating people identically and treating them fairly lead to the same result. Equality also has practical virtues. It is easy to calculate and easy to check, and it spares the group from having to judge whose needs or efforts count for more. Those virtues help explain why equal division is so often accepted without discussion.

The fairness of the first division therefore rested on conditions that nobody stated. Equal shares were fair because the people involved were similar in the respects that mattered: what they had contributed and what they needed. Equality did not create fairness by itself; it matched a situation in which there were no relevant differences to respond to. Seen this way, the absence of complaint on the first evening was not evidence that equality is always fair. It was evidence that, in that case, nothing called for a different rule.

The second evening altered those conditions. One colleague had paid for most of the order because the others were short of cash. Another had skipped lunch and was far hungrier than the rest. Dividing the pizza equally now ignored two differences at once. The colleague who had paid could reasonably claim that her contribution deserved recognition, and the hungry colleague could reasonably claim that his need deserved priority. The same method that produced agreement under the first set of conditions produced disagreement under the second.

These two claims cannot be settled simply by replacing equality with some other rule, because they point in different directions. A division based on contribution would give more to the colleague who paid; a division based on need would give more to the one who was hungry. Neither claim is obviously mistaken, and neither can be translated into the other. Need looks forward to what a person requires, while contribution looks back to what a person has done. Fairness, in other words, may involve several principles that do not reduce to a single scale.

A fictional case on a larger scale tests whether this pattern holds. Imagine a small town, here called Merrow, cut off by a flood for several days. Relief workers arrive with limited water, blankets, and building materials. Giving each household an equal package is quick and visibly impartial, which matters in the first hours, before anyone knows who needs what, and when people fear favoritism. Yet households differ in size, some include infants or people who are ill, and some residents spend long hours repairing shared roads. Equal packages would overlook all of these differences, as equal slices did on the second evening.

Merrow also shows that different principles may suit different goods. Water could reasonably be divided per person, since each person needs a similar amount. Medicine would follow need, because medicine handed to the healthy is wasted. Building materials might go first to the households with the most damage, or partly to those who help repair the roads. The lesson of the pizza still holds: equality is fair where relevant differences are absent. But the town adds a qualification, since which differences are relevant depends on the good being divided.

What can be concluded from these cases is limited but useful. Equal division is fair when people are alike in the respects that matter, or when those respects cannot yet be known. Where need and contribution clearly differ, fairness requires attention to them, and different goods may call for different principles. The cases do not show how to weigh a strong claim of need against a strong claim of contribution when the two conflict over the same good. On that question no single rule emerged, and none should be assumed.

passage.title: Why Some Birds Copy Their Neighbors

paragraphs.text: Imagine walking across a large park in spring and listening to the males of a single songbird species. On the eastern side, most of them end their songs with a quick trill; on the western side, with a few slower notes. Within each side, neighbors sound remarkably alike. Local patterns of this kind, sometimes called dialects, have been described in a number of songbird species. They raise a simple question: why should birds living close together share a version of a song that birds farther away do not?

Answering that question requires sorting the possible causes. Neighbors might sound alike because they are related and have inherited similar tendencies. They might sound alike because each young bird learned its song by listening to the adults around it. Or the local surroundings, such as dense vegetation or background noise, might favor certain sounds in every bird living there. A practical way to separate the first two causes is to ask whether a bird develops a normal song without hearing others, and whether its song changes when it lives among different singers.

Many songbirds fall clearly on the learning side. In these species, young males raised without hearing adult song tend to develop songs that are simplified or abnormal, while young birds exposed to recordings of adults often copy what they hear. Learning usually takes place during a limited period early in life, after which the song becomes relatively fixed. Under these conditions, local similarity is easy to explain: young birds copy the adults they hear, and small differences between areas are passed on in much the same way that human accents are.

Other birds fall on the opposite side. In some groups, including certain flycatchers, individuals raised without hearing their own species still produce songs that sound normal. For such birds, similarity among neighbors says little about copying, since a member of the species would produce roughly the same song wherever it grew up. Comparing these two kinds of species suggests a second criterion: inherited songs tend to sound alike across a species' whole range, while learned songs can differ from place to place, as the birds in the park appear to do.

Local variation, however, does not settle the matter. Young birds of many species settle fairly close to where they hatched, so neighbors are often relatives. A local version of a song could, in principle, reflect an inherited tendency shared within related families as well as a learned tradition. In such populations, both explanations predict the same pattern of neighbors sounding alike and distant birds sounding different. The boundary between the categories is blurred here not because the categories are meaningless, but because the usual observations cannot tell them apart.

Birds that arrive from elsewhere offer a way to test the categories. If an immigrant that is unrelated to its new neighbors comes to sing the local version, learning must be involved, since it could not have inherited that variant from local families. If it keeps the song of its birthplace, the result is more ambiguous. That might reflect an inherited song, but it might equally reflect learning that occurred before the bird moved, during the early period when songs become fixed. Watching immigrants therefore refines the classification: the timing of learning matters as much as whether learning occurs at all.

The classification remains useful for some purposes. It helps researchers decide which species are suited to studies of song traditions and which are not. It becomes misleading, however, when it is treated as a strict choice between genes and learning. Even in species that learn, young birds tend to copy the songs of their own species more readily than other sounds, which suggests that inherited tendencies shape what is learned. A species can belong on the learning side while still depending on inheritance for its capacity to learn.

Why, then, do some birds copy their neighbors? The answer depends on more than one kind of evidence. Similarity among neighbors is where the inquiry begins, not where it ends. The case for cultural transmission becomes strong when birds raised without adult models develop abnormal songs, when unrelated newcomers adopt the local variant, and when such variants persist across generations of birds that are not closely related. Where these observations are found together, it is reasonable to say that birds learn from their neighbors; where only similarity is found, the question remains open.

passage.title: The Workers Absent from a Factory Museum

paragraphs.text: At the center of many industrial heritage exhibits stands a polished machine. In a restored textile mill, it might be a power loom, its iron frame freshly painted and its moving parts demonstrated twice a day for visitors. On the wall nearby hangs a portrait of the mill's founder, with a panel describing his investments and the town that grew up around his factory. Elsewhere in the same building, if it has been kept at all, lies a far less striking object: a page from a pay ledger, filled with names written in a clerk's hurried hand.

These objects can be read as answers to different questions. The loom and the portrait answer the question of how production was organized and who directed it. The ledger answers the question of who did the work and on what terms. The difference between them is not simply one of importance. It reflects which records were created deliberately, by whom, and which ones survived. That criterion, the origin and survival of evidence, makes it possible to compare the two accounts fairly rather than treating one as the true story and the other as an afterthought.

The account centered on machines and managers rests on abundant material. Companies kept board minutes, correspondence with investors, and annual reports, and these were often preserved in archives or donated by founding families. Machines themselves are durable and visually impressive, which makes them natural centerpieces. This account is not false. It accurately describes technological change and the decisions that shaped a factory town. Its limitation lies in what its sources were designed to record: output, costs and plans, rather than the daily experience of the people who operated the machines.

An account centered on workers must draw on thinner and more scattered evidence. In many mill towns, a large share of the workforce came from abroad, often recruited as earlier groups of workers left or demanded better pay. These newcomers frequently spoke languages that managers did not read, moved between jobs and towns, and lived in housing that company records barely described. Few had the time or means to keep diaries, and the letters they sent home were usually kept, if at all, in another country.

Their absence from exhibits is therefore partly a problem of evidence and partly a problem of selection. Material about immigrant workers was less likely to be produced, and less likely to be kept, than material about owners. Yet even surviving traces were often left out when museums were first designed, because a story of invention and enterprise seemed more coherent and more flattering to the town. The result is an exhibit in which the machines appear to run by themselves, guided only by the decisions of the people in the portraits.

Pay ledgers and oral histories can begin to correct this imbalance, though in different ways. A ledger records names, wages, hours, fines for lateness or damaged cloth, and how long each worker stayed. It can reveal patterns that no single memory could, such as how often workers left within their first year. Yet ledgers say nothing about how anyone felt, and clerks often misspelled or shortened foreign names. Oral histories, collected from former workers or their children, supply feeling and detail, but they were often recorded decades later, mostly from people who stayed in the area, and are shaped by later experience.

The line between the two accounts is not perfectly sharp. Company records sometimes discuss workers at length, for example in reports on strikes or complaints, though always from management's point of view. Some immigrant communities, meanwhile, produced their own newspapers, church registers and union minutes, which offer a perspective that neither ledgers nor managers provide. Whether such sources exist for a particular town depends on local circumstances, so the size of the gap cannot be judged in the same way everywhere.

Placed side by side, the loom and the ledger show that every record is selective, including those that seem most complete. What can be stated with confidence is that an exhibit centered on machines and managers reflects which records were made and kept, not who contributed to production. What remains uncertain is how much of the missing experience can be recovered. Ledgers and oral histories can restore names, patterns and some voices, but many workers left traces too faint for any museum to reconstruct their lives in full.

passage.title: Why Demand Matters as Much as Supply

paragraphs.text: On the kitchen wall of a house with solar panels, a small screen draws two lines through the day. One shows how much electricity the roof is producing; the other shows how much the household is using. Around noon, the production line rises well above the consumption line, and the surplus flows out to the grid. By early evening the picture reverses. The sun drops, the panels fall silent, and the family comes home to cook, switch on lights, and run the heating or cooling. The two lines cross, and the house begins to draw power from elsewhere.

It is tempting to ignore that crossing and think only about totals. If a single roof can produce more than its household needs at midday, then a region that keeps adding solar farms and wind turbines should eventually have power to spare. The idea is simple and attractive: build enough renewable capacity, and supply problems will disappear. Treated as a hypothesis rather than a certainty, it can be checked against what grids with large amounts of renewable generation actually experience.

Some observable facts do fit it. Where renewable capacity has grown quickly, the amount of electricity generated from wind and sunlight over a year has risen substantially. On sunny days, solar output in such systems can be so large that wholesale prices fall very low around midday, and operators sometimes curtail production, instructing some solar or wind plants to reduce output because the grid cannot use it all at that moment.

These facts support one part of the hypothesis. Adding capacity clearly raises the total quantity of energy that can be produced, and annual figures show that renewable sources can supply a large share of a region's yearly consumption. A grid that once depended almost entirely on fuel-burning plants can, in this sense, become far less dependent on them. If the question were only how much energy a region can produce over twelve months, the evidence would point strongly toward building more.

What annual totals cannot show is timing. Electricity on a grid must be balanced moment by moment; power produced at noon cannot serve a kitchen at seven in the evening unless it is stored somewhere in between. Curtailment, which might look like a sign of abundance, actually reveals the problem: surplus at one hour can exist alongside shortage at another. As solar output fades in the late afternoon while demand climbs toward its evening peak, other sources must increase their output quickly. Adding more solar panels enlarges the midday surplus but does little for those evening hours.

Two remedies address the gap in different ways. Storage, usually in the form of large batteries, moves energy across time: it charges when power is plentiful and discharges when it is scarce. Its limits are how many hours it can supply, the energy lost in each cycle, and its cost, and it helps little during several days of calm, cloudy weather. Demand shifting moves use instead of supply. Water heaters, electric car chargers, and some industrial processes can run at midday rather than in the evening. This requires no large equipment, but it depends on whether people and appliances can actually adjust, and some needs, like cooking dinner, cannot easily move.

The original hypothesis is not wrong everywhere. In a region where strong winds tend to blow in the evening, or where demand peaks in the hot afternoon because of air conditioning, renewable output may already follow demand closely. A grid with large reservoirs behind hydroelectric dams can also hold water back during sunny hours and release it later. Under such conditions, adding capacity alone might go a long way. The strength of the hypothesis therefore depends on the shape of local demand and the mix of available resources, not on capacity as such.

Some conclusions can be stated firmly. Total generation and usable power are different quantities, and the second depends on whether supply matches demand in time. Annual figures cannot settle whether a grid will meet its evening peak. Other questions remain uncertain: which combination of storage, flexible demand, and further capacity suits a particular region, how readily people will change their habits, and how costs will develop. The two lines on the kitchen screen capture the firm part well. They do not, by themselves, answer the uncertain part.

passage.title: A Course Designed Around Mistakes

paragraphs.text: Language classrooms have changed their attitude toward errors more than once. Drill-based methods that were popular in the mid-twentieth century often aimed to prevent mistakes altogether, on the reasoning that every error practiced was a bad habit in the making. Later approaches placed more weight on communication and treated errors as a normal part of learning. The fictional course described here, an introductory evening class in Portuguese at a community center, was designed in the earlier spirit, although its organizers did not think of it in those terms.

In its first term, each lesson followed the same pattern. The instructor modeled a sentence, learners repeated it together, and then individuals were called on to produce variations. Any error was corrected immediately, in front of the group, and the learner repeated the corrected form. The organizers had chosen this approach for a sensible reason. Many participants were adults preparing for short trips abroad, with little time to unlearn wrong forms, and accuracy from the very start seemed the most efficient route.

Behind this design lay a familiar idea: errors are signs of failure, and learning goes best when failure is kept to a minimum. There is something to this. Repeating an incorrect form many times can make it harder to change, and a learner who never receives correction may not notice a persistent mistake. The idea quietly assumes, however, that learners will keep speaking under such conditions, so that the correct forms actually get practiced.

A second scene, from a different fictional group, offers a contrast. In a conversation club that met in the same building, learners of varying levels chatted in pairs about their weekend plans, borrowing words from their first language when they got stuck. Nobody corrected them during these conversations. Mistakes were frequent and some went unnoticed, but the room was full of attempts, and learners often tried out phrases they had heard only once.

Placing the two scenes side by side reveals the problem the course faced. By the middle of the first term, instructors noticed that many learners answered only when they were certain, kept their sentences short, or avoided volunteering at all. In the club, adults with similar backgrounds spoke readily. The course had reduced visible errors, but it may also have reduced the amount of speaking through which learners could test and extend what they knew. For many of them, hesitation rather than inaccuracy had become the main obstacle.

In the second term, the instructors changed two things. They added brief pair activities in which mistakes carried no public consequence, and they moved most correction to the end of each activity, reviewing common errors with the whole class without naming who had made them. Learners spoke noticeably more, and instructors reported that certain errors appeared less often in later weeks. Because both changes were introduced together and the course kept no comparison group, however, it was impossible to tell which change mattered more, or whether the extra speaking alone explained the improvement.

Seen again in this light, a learner corrected in front of the group during the first term looks different. The correction itself was accurate and probably useful. What shaped the learner's behavior may have been its timing and visibility, which turned each attempt into a small public test. The idea behind the original design was therefore not simply mistaken, since correction still had value. What mattered was when and how errors were treated, not merely whether they were treated at all.

The observations from this fictional course are modest: learners spoke more after the changes, and certain errors became less frequent. The interpretation that mistakes themselves have learning value goes further. It fits what happened, since learners who risked more errors also improved, but the course did not show that making errors caused the improvement, as opposed to the extra practice that came with them. What the case does support is narrower. Avoiding mistakes and learning from them are different goals, and a course can pursue the first at the expense of the second.

passage.title: The Lighthouse Records That Revealed Trade

paragraphs.text: During the nineteenth century, many states began counting their trade with new thoroughness. Customs offices recorded the goods passing through major ports and the duties collected on them, and these figures were gathered into annual tables. In the same period, lighthouses multiplied along busy coasts. Their keepers kept logbooks, mainly to show that the lamp had been lit and to note storms and wrecks, but at some stations they also wrote down passing vessels. For a long time, historians treated the first kind of record as a source on the economy and the second as a source on lighthouses.

The division rested on a sensible intuition: to learn how much trade a region carried on, consult the official statistics. Customs tables were produced by trained clerks following set rules, they covered many years in a consistent format, and they were tied to revenue that governments cared about collecting. A keeper's notes, by contrast, were written by one person on a remote headland, with no standard form and no obvious economic purpose. Where the official figures showed little activity, it seemed reasonable to conclude that little activity had taken place.

Consider, as an illustration, a historian who works through the log of a lighthouse overlooking a minor harbor and counts every vessel the keepers recorded over several decades. The entries are brief, often giving only the time, the direction of travel, and a word describing the type of craft. Yet the totals are striking. Small sailing vessels pass almost daily in some months, sightings rise in late summer and autumn, and over the decades studied the overall count holds steady or grows slightly rather than falling away.

The official statistics for the same harbor tell another story. Its recorded trade is modest throughout and declines toward the end of the period, as larger ships concentrate at a few major ports. If the customs tables give a complete picture, the coast was becoming economically quieter. If the lighthouse log reflects real traffic, something kept a steady stream of small vessels moving past the headland. The two records cannot both be taken at face value as measures of the same activity.

Several explanations could reconcile them. Perhaps many of the passing craft were fishing boats rather than traders, so their numbers say little about commerce. Perhaps the keepers' habits changed, with later keepers recording vessels more diligently than earlier ones, creating an apparent stability that hides a real decline. Or perhaps the vessels were carrying goods between ports within the same country, traffic that customs officials may have recorded separately, lightly, or not at all, because it was not subject to the duties the tables were designed to track.

These explanations can be tested against details in the log and in other records. If the boats were mostly fishing, sightings should peak with the fishing season, but in this illustration they peak instead after harvests, when bulk goods such as grain were typically moved. If the keepers' diligence changed, the pattern should shift when one keeper replaced another, yet it continues smoothly across several changes of staff. Harbor dues paid by small vessels, recorded by the town rather than by customs, point in the same direction. The most consistent reading is that a coastal trade existed largely outside the official categories.

This does not mean the customs tables were wrong about what they measured. For trade with foreign ports, where duties were collected and goods carefully valued, they remain the better source, and the lighthouse log adds little. The log also has limits of its own. It counts passing vessels, not cargo, so it cannot say how much was carried or what it was worth, and a single headland observes only one stretch of coast. The old intuition, in short, still holds for the kind of trade the official system was built to see.

What changes is the picture of how the regional economy was structured. Instead of a few major ports surrounded by inactive coastline, the combined evidence suggests a dense network of small exchanges linking minor harbors, which official statistics largely missed because of how their categories were defined. How large that network was in money terms remains uncertain, and one lighthouse cannot show whether the same pattern held elsewhere. The case shows, more modestly, that records kept for other purposes can reveal economic activity that the main sources were never designed to capture.

passage.title: The Anonymous Dataset That Wasn't

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, keeping people unidentifiable in published records was treated as a matter of deletion. Names, street addresses, and identification numbers were removed, and what remained was considered safe to share. Records were mostly printed in tables, other collections of personal information were hard to obtain, and under those conditions deletion offered meaningful protection. Both conditions have since changed: data are released in files that computers can search, and many other datasets are freely available online. Consider the Halden Health Institute, an organization invented for this discussion, which publishes a dataset it calls anonymous. Is that accurate?

By the most familiar measure, it is. The institute's team checked every column and removed anything that names a person directly. Each record contains only a birth year, sex, a five-digit postal code, the month of a hospital visit, and the diagnosis recorded at that visit. Under this standard, the question is whether any single field points to an individual, and none does. If anonymity means the absence of direct identifiers, the release passes.

A second measure asks a different question: how many records are unique when several ordinary details are considered together? Birth year, sex, and postal code each describe large groups of people, but combined they can narrow a group sharply. In a postal area with a few thousand residents, there may be only one man born in a particular year who visited a hospital in a particular month. Examined this way, a large share of the institute's records have combinations that occur only once. By this measure, many records are anonymous in name only.

The two measures therefore reach opposite verdicts about the same file. The first examines fields one at a time and finds nothing identifying. The second examines combinations and finds that many records stand alone. Neither measure is mistaken about what it counts. They disagree because they define the risk differently: one asks whether a record carries a label, the other whether it can be singled out. A dataset can satisfy the first standard completely while performing poorly on the second, and an institute that reports only the first may sincerely believe it has protected everyone.

Uniqueness alone does not reveal who a person is, and here evaluation becomes more treacherous. A unique combination becomes a name only when it can be matched with another source that contains the same details together with an identity. Public registers, news reports, and personal posts online can supply exactly that. Someone who knows that an acquaintance born in a certain year lives in a certain postal area and was hospitalized last spring could find the single matching record and learn the diagnosis. The risk thus depends not only on the file but on what other information exists, which the institute neither controls nor fully knows.

Suppose the institute responds by changing the level of detail. Birth years are grouped into ten-year bands, postal codes are shortened to their first three digits, and visit months are combined into seasons. Measured by uniqueness, the effect is dramatic: most combinations now describe dozens or hundreds of people. Measured by usefulness to researchers, there is a cost, since patterns visible only at fine scales, such as a local outbreak, may disappear. Measured against linkage, the change helps but guarantees nothing, because someone who knows other details, such as a rare diagnosis, may still narrow the group to one.

Each measure serves a particular purpose. Checking for direct identifiers is quick and catches obvious errors. Counting unique combinations estimates how easily records could be singled out. Considering possible linkages comes closest to the real risk, yet it requires assumptions about information that may not exist yet. A dataset judged safe today could become identifiable when a new public source appears tomorrow. No single number, then, settles whether a release is anonymous.

Was the Halden dataset anonymous, then? Under the old standard of deletion, yes; under a standard of uniqueness, largely not; and under a standard of linkage, the answer depends on what others know and may later publish. What the case shows is that anonymity is not a property a file possesses on its own. It is a judgment that depends on the measure chosen and on the data surrounding the file, and changing the level of detail shifts that judgment without making it final.

choices.text_ja: 同じ生まれ年と性別をもつ、ほかの多数の記録。

choices.text_ja: 公開されたファイルそのものの中で一度しか現れない項目の組み合わせ。

choices.text_ja: 同じ情報と身元とをあわせて含む別の情報源との照合。

questions.stem: What does the change in the level of detail described in paragraph 6 achieve?

choices.text: It greatly reduces the linkage risk while keeping fine-scale patterns visible to researchers.
choices.text_ja: 照合の危険を大幅に減らしつつ、細かい単位のパターンを研究者に見える状態に保つ。

choices.text: It makes records much harder to single out but cannot rule out identification.
choices.text_ja: 記録を一つに特定することをはるかに難しくするが、個人の特定を排除することはできない。

choices.text: It raises the file's usefulness to researchers but leaves uniqueness largely unchanged.
choices.text_ja: ファイルの研究者にとっての有用性を高めるが、ほかと重ならない記録の多さはほとんど変わらない。

choices.text: It makes it unnecessary to remove direct identifiers from the published file.
choices.text_ja: 公開ファイルから直接的な識別子を取り除く必要をなくす。

questions.stem_ja: 第6段落で述べられている情報の細かさの変更は、何をもたらすか。

questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 2 through 4, why might an institute sincerely but wrongly believe its data were anonymous?

choices.text: It may have counted unique combinations but overlooked direct identifiers.
choices.text_ja: ほかと重ならない組み合わせは数えたが、直接的な識別子を見落としたのかもしれないから。

choices.text: It may have assumed that postal codes identify people less often than names.
choices.text_ja: 郵便番号は氏名ほど人を特定しないと仮定していたのかもしれないから。

choices.text: It may have relied on public registers that contained outdated information.
choices.text_ja: 古い情報を含む公的な名簿に頼っていたのかもしれないから。

choices.text: It may have checked fields individually without examining their combinations.
choices.text_ja: 項目を一つずつ確認しただけで、その組み合わせを調べなかったのかもしれないから。

questions.stem_ja: 第2段落から第4段落に基づくと、研究所が自らのデータは匿名だと、本気で、しかし誤って信じてしまうことがあるのはなぜか。

questions.stem: According to the passage, why could a dataset judged safe today become identifiable later?

choices.text: Newly published sources supply details that link its records to identities.
choices.text_ja: 新たに公開された情報源が、その記録を身元と結びつける情報を提供するから。

choices.text: Checks for direct identifiers tend to become less reliable as file formats change.
choices.text_ja: ファイル形式が変わるにつれて、直接的な識別子の確認は信頼性が下がる傾向があるから。

choices.text: The number of unique combinations in a released file tends to grow over time.
choices.text_ja: 公開されたファイルの中の、ほかと重ならない組み合わせの数は時とともに増える傾向があるから。

choices.text: Coarser grouping of categories tends to lose its effect once data are reused.
choices.text_ja: 区分をより粗くまとめることは、データが再利用されると効果を失う傾向があるから。

passage.title: Can a Wildlife Corridor Become a Trap?

paragraphs.text: Whether a strip of habitat built to help animals move between forests can end up drawing them into danger is a question that ordinary field records can answer, at least in part. To see how, consider an invented case. Two forest blocks, here called the North Wood and the South Wood, are separated by farmland and a two-lane road. A planted corridor of hedges and young trees links them, designed so that small mammals and deer can travel from one block to the other under cover.

The planners' reasoning was straightforward. Animals confined to a single forest block can lose genetic variety over generations, and a local population may vanish if disease or fire strikes. A corridor offers cover, so animals that avoid open fields can still cross. The plan, however, required the corridor to meet the road at one point, where no bridge or tunnel was originally built. The designers assumed that traffic was light enough for the occasional animal to cross safely.

The first evidence came from camera traps placed along the corridor. Over several seasons, they recorded far more animals moving through the planted strip than had been recorded crossing the open fields before it existed. This shows that the corridor was being used and that it channeled movement along a single route. It does not show where the animals went after leaving the cameras' view, nor whether those movements led to successful settlement or breeding in the other forest.

The second evidence came from a different method: volunteers walked the road and recorded animals killed by traffic. Their records showed that collisions had become concentrated near the point where the corridor met the road, whereas before the corridor, deaths at that spot had been fewer and scattered. Taken alone, this record might suggest that the corridor was simply harmful. Yet roadkill counts depend on how carefully a stretch is searched, and the volunteers may have searched near the corridor more often because they knew it was being studied.

At first glance, the two kinds of evidence disagree. One suggests that the corridor succeeded in increasing movement; the other suggests that it increased deaths. But they may describe a single process. A corridor that gathers animals into a narrow path will, if that path ends at a road, also gather them at one crossing point. More movement and more collisions would then be two consequences of the same design feature rather than contradictory findings about whether the corridor worked.

The corridor's managers tested this interpretation by changing the design. They built an underpass beneath the road at the corridor's end, added fencing to guide animals toward it, and moved new plantings away from a stretch where the corridor had led animals out beside the traffic. Afterward, cameras in the underpass recorded regular use, and the volunteers, still searching as often as before, found fewer dead animals near the corridor. The pattern fits the idea that the problem lay in where the corridor delivered animals, not in the existence of the corridor itself.

Other explanations cannot be fully excluded. Traffic volume might have fallen during the same period, or a decline in local deer numbers might have reduced both crossings and collisions. The managers had no comparison site where nothing was changed, so the improvement cannot be credited with certainty to the underpass. Some species, moreover, may refuse to enter tunnels and continue to cross on the surface, a possibility that the underpass cameras, by their placement, could not reveal.

So can a corridor become a trap? The evidence from this case suggests that it can, but not because connecting habitats is harmful in itself. The danger arose where the corridor concentrated movement and then released it onto a road. What has been learned is that connectivity should be judged by its quality, including where a link leads and what animals encounter along the way, rather than by the mere presence of a link on a map. Whether the redesign has fully removed the danger is still an open question.

questions.stem: What feature of the original design made the opening question relevant?

choices.text: The corridor linked two forests that already shared one large population.
choices.text_ja: 回廊が、すでに一つの大きな個体群を共有していた二つの森をつないでいた。

choices.text: The corridor was planted with trees too young to provide any cover.
choices.text_ja: 回廊に植えられた木が若すぎて、身を隠す場所にならなかった。

choices.text: The corridor ran through farmland that animals already crossed easily.
choices.text_ja: 回廊が、動物がすでに容易に横切っていた農地を通っていた。

choices.text: The corridor met the road at one point that had no crossing structure.
choices.text_ja: 回廊が、横断施設のない1か所で道路に接していた。

questions.stem_ja: 当初の設計のどのような特徴が、冒頭の問いを意味あるものにしたか。

questions.stem: What can the camera-trap evidence establish on its own?

choices.text: Animals that used the corridor settled and bred in the other forest.
choices.text_ja: 回廊を利用した動物は、もう一方の森で定着し繁殖した。

choices.text: Animals used the corridor more than they had crossed the open fields.
choices.text_ja: 動物は、以前開けた畑を横切っていた以上に回廊を利用していた。

choices.text: Animals killed on the road had entered it from the end of the corridor.
choices.text_ja: 道路で死んだ動物は、回廊の終点から道路に入っていた。

choices.text: Animals avoided the corridor in seasons when road traffic was heavy.
choices.text_ja: 道路の交通量が多い季節には、動物は回廊を避けていた。

questions.stem_ja: 自動撮影カメラの証拠だけで立証できることは何か。

questions.stem: Why does the author warn against treating the roadkill record alone as proof of harm?

choices.text: Deaths near the corridor were fewer than those recorded along the rest of the road.
choices.text_ja: 回廊付近での死亡は、道路のほかの区間で記録された死亡より少なかったから。

choices.text: Collisions had already been concentrated at that spot before the corridor existed.
choices.text_ja: 回廊ができる前から、衝突はすでにその地点に集中していたから。

choices.text: Volunteers counted only deer and ignored the small mammals using the corridor.
choices.text_ja: ボランティアはシカだけを数え、回廊を使う小型哺乳類を無視していたから。

choices.text: Searching more often near the corridor may have raised the recorded deaths.
choices.text_ja: 回廊付近をより頻繁に探したことで、記録された死亡数が増えた可能性があるから。

questions.stem_ja: 筆者が、路上の死骸の記録だけを害の証拠とみなすことに注意を促しているのはなぜか。

questions.stem: How does the redesign help reconcile the two kinds of evidence?

choices.text: Collisions fell while search effort stayed steady, tying both findings to the crossing.
choices.text_ja: 探す頻度が変わらないまま衝突が減り、両方の発見が横断地点に結びつけられた。

choices.text: The fencing revealed that cameras had counted the same animals repeatedly.
choices.text_ja: 柵によって、カメラが同じ動物を繰り返し数えていたことが明らかになった。

choices.text: Moving the plantings showed that the corridor had never increased movement.
choices.text_ja: 植栽を移したことで、回廊が移動を増やしたことは一度もなかったと分かった。

choices.text: The underpass cut movement through the corridor, which in turn lowered collisions.
choices.text_ja: 地下通路が回廊を通る移動を減らし、その結果として衝突が減った。

questions.stem_ja: 設計の変更は、二種類の証拠を整合させるのにどのように役立つか。

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the passage's conclusion and its limits?

choices.text: Where a corridor leads matters, though the underpass's effect cannot be confirmed.
choices.text_ja: 回廊がどこへ通じるかが重要だが、地下通路の効果は確証できない。

choices.text: Falling traffic, rather than the redesign, explains the drop in collisions.
choices.text_ja: 衝突の減少は、設計の変更ではなく交通量の減少によって説明される。

choices.text: Corridors concentrate animals and are harmful, so links should usually be avoided.
choices.text_ja: 回廊は動物を集中させて有害なので、つながりはたいてい避けるべきである。

choices.text: The redesign solved the problem for all species, as the underpass cameras showed.
choices.text_ja: 地下通路のカメラが示したとおり、設計の変更はすべての種について問題を解決した。

questions.stem_ja: 本文の結論とその限界を最もよく反映している記述はどれか。
